decision_governed: B22/B21: the MR arm adjusts for AGE ONLY, not the observational confounder set (age+gravidity+BMI+education). PCs would also be legitimate but no adequate PCA exists (see docs/paths_reference.md).
verbatim_quote: In general, we recommend only including as covariates age, sex, genomic principal components of ancestry, and technical covariates (such as recruitment centre), as further adjustment may bias estimates either if adjustment is for a variable on the causal pathway from the genetic variants to the outcome (a mediator), or if adjustment induces collider bias.
caveat: Phrased as "in general, we recommend" - guidance, not a prohibition. BMI/education/gravidity are OUR examples of covariates falling outside the recommended set; the paper names only the categories to include. Statement appears once, in the one-sample/2SLS section.
source: Burgess S, Davey Smith G, Davies NM, Dudbridge F, Gill D, Glymour MM, Hartwig FP, Kutalik Z, Holmes MV, Minelli C, Morrison JV, Pan W, Relton CL, Theodoratou E. Guidelines for performing Mendelian randomization investigations: update for summer 2023. Wellcome Open Research 2019;4:186 (v3, 2023)

decision_governed: B22: the first stage (BP ~ z) and reduced form (Y ~ z) must use the SAME covariate set, or the Wald ratio is incoherent.
verbatim_quote: In the first stage, the exposure is regressed on the genetic variants and any relevant covariates. In the second stage the outcome is then regressed on the predicted values of the exposure from the first regression and the same covariates.
caveat: Stated for 2SLS specifically; the ratio-estimator form we use is algebraically equivalent for a single instrument.
source: Burgess S et al., Wellcome Open Research 2019;4:186 (v3, 2023)

decision_governed: T2: R2pct_disatt corrects observed R2 for BP measurement error. Uses reliability of the MEAN of k readings (Spearman-Brown), NOT the single-reading ICC - the latter over-corrected by ~2x.
verbatim_quote: Correction for attenuation is a statistical procedure, due to Spearman (1904), to rid a correlation coefficient from the weakening effect of measurement error, a phenomenon also known as regression dilution.
caveat: Applies to R2 only. Measurement error in an OUTCOME does not bias the slope, so beta (mmHg per SD) and F are unbiased and must NOT be corrected. Standard in psychometrics and meta-analysis.
source: Spearman C (1904), via Wikipedia "Correction for attenuation"

decision_governed: Justifies correcting BP-based R2 at all: a single BP reading is a poor measure of usual BP.
verbatim_quote: After correction for this regression dilution bias, prolonged differences in usual diastolic blood pressure of 5, 7.5, and 10 mm Hg were respectively associated with at least 34%, 46%, and 56% less stroke
caveat: Landmark is for BP as EXPOSURE (slope attenuation); our T2 use is BP as OUTCOME (R2 attenuation only). Same phenomenon, different quantity affected. NB MR is naturally immune: noise in the first-stage outcome does not bias the slope, so the Wald ratio already estimates the effect of TRUE BP.
source: MacMahon S et al. Blood pressure, stroke, and coronary heart disease. Part 1. Lancet 1990;335:765-74

decision_governed: S15/B32: whether the maternal BP->birthweight association is an intrauterine maternal effect or the transmitted fetal alleles acting on the fetus. Our decomposition attenuates the maternal coefficient 37-50%; we report this as a LIMITATION of our power, not as a finding, because this study found the opposite with far greater power.
verbatim_quote: MR analyses indicated that a 1SD (10mmHg) higher maternal SBP is causally associated with a 0.15 SD (95%CI: -0.19, -0.11) lower offspring birth weight, independent of the direct fetal effects. In contrast, there was no fetal effect of SBP on their own birth weight, after adjusting for the indirect maternal effect (-0.01 SD per 10mmHg, 95% CI: -0.05, 0.03)
caveat: Their SEM was validated against conditional regression in 18,873 mother-offspring pairs; we have 8,711. Evans et al. (IJE 2019;48:861-875) report being unable to resolve maternal from fetal effects at N=12,909. Warrington also state "we have not considered paternal genotypes, and it is possible that this omission has biased the results of some of our analyses" - the same gap applies to us and bites harder at our N. NB our UNCONDITIONAL estimate (-0.165 SD/10 mmHg, SAS) closely matches their CONDITIONAL maternal estimate (-0.15), which is what you would expect if there were little real fetal contribution to remove.
source: Warrington NM, Beaumont RN, Horikoshi M, et al. Maternal and fetal genetic effects on birth weight and their relevance to cardio-metabolic risk factors. Nat Genet 2019;51(5):804-814

topic: Offspring genotype violates the exclusion restriction
decision_governed: B32 exists at all: in MR of a MATERNAL exposure on an OFFSPRING outcome, the mother-offspring genotype correlation of ~0.5 means the maternal genetic association captures both an intrauterine maternal effect and the effect of transmitted alleles in the fetus.
verbatim_quote: A specific way in which the exclusion restriction assumption may be violated in studies of the effects of maternal pregnancy exposures on offspring outcomes, is via the offspring's genetic variants
caveat: Their recommendation is to adjust for offspring genotype in the MAIN analysis and, if possible, paternal genotype simultaneously. We do the former and cannot do the latter.
source: Lawlor D, Richmond R, Warrington N, McMahon G, Davey Smith G, Bowden J, Evans DM. Using Mendelian randomization to determine causal effects of maternal pregnancy (intrauterine) exposures on offspring outcomes. Wellcome Open Res 2017;2:11
